summary: This document describes a threat model for the setting in which External BGP path security mechanisms will be developed. It analyzes the RPKI and focuses on an Autonomous System's ability to verify the authenticity of the AS path information it receives.

plainLanguage.summary: Path security would let a router check that the list of networks a route passed through is genuine. This RFC asks who might try to break that: other network operators, hackers, criminals, registry staff and governments. For each it lists what they could attack and what they could get away with.

questions: how can as path be forged
subtitle: Who could attack BGP path security, and what they could do if they did.

tldr.problem: Path security for BGP is a family of designs that protect the AS_PATH attribute of a route update. Before anyone builds one, the designers need to know who might attack it and what they would try.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines PATHSEC and the AS-centric model it works in, then names five classes of adversary: network operators, hackers, criminals, registries and nations. It then works through the attacks each could mount, grouped by their target: the sessions between routers, a BGP router, the operator's management computers, a repository publication point and a certification authority.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational RFC that defines no protocol. Its last section lists the vulnerabilities that path security leaves open, including route leaks, other path attributes, and the risk that a relying party acts on stale repository data.

facts.label: Adversary classes
facts.value: Network operators, hackers, criminals, registries, nations

today: RFC 7132 is an Informational RFC published in February 2014. It has not been obsoleted or updated. It remains the threat model for BGP path security, describing the adversaries, the attacks and the residual vulnerabilities.

sections.title: What Path Security Is For
sections.content:
The term PATHSEC, for path security, refers to any design used to preserve the integrity and authenticity of the AS_PATH attribute carried in a BGP update message. The security context comes from the Secure Inter-Domain Routing working group charter, which requires that solutions affording path security make use of the Resource Public Key Infrastructure, and that they protect only the information needed to verify that a received route traversed the Autonomous Systems in question and that the address prefix in the route is what was advertised. The goal of path security is therefore to let a BGP speaker verify that the ASes enumerated in the path attribute really are the sequence of ASes the prefix traversed.

The motivation is a set of residual security concerns about BGP. BGP has no mechanism by which an AS can verify the legitimacy and authenticity of route advertisements, and BGP speakers can inject bogus routing information either by masquerading as another speaker or by distributing unauthorized information as themselves. Historically, misconfigured and faulty routers have caused widespread disruption, and legitimate peers have the context and information to produce believable but bogus routing information. The cryptographic protection of the session between peers cannot exclude that.

Path security is meant to build on what the RPKI already offers, which is route origination validation: relying parties can already determine whether the origin AS of a path was authorised to advertise the prefix in an update, using a public key infrastructure that associates prefixes with the keys of address space holders, and route origin authorisations that let a prefix holder name the ASes allowed to originate routes for it.

One design choice shapes everything that follows. The security model does not assume an oracle that can see all the BGP input and output of every AS or router. Instead it rests on a local notion of what counts as legitimate, authorised behaviour by the routers of an AS. That is an AS-centric model of secure operation, matching the AS-centric model BGP already uses for routing.
sections.plainLanguage: Path security is about one thing: proving that the list of networks a route passed through is the real list. The RFC assumes no central witness, so each router can only judge what its own neighbours did.

sections.title: The Terms Used
sections.content:
The RFC defines the vocabulary the rest of the document depends on, and the definitions are deliberately narrow.

An adversary is an entity, such as a person or an organisation, perceived as malicious relative to the security policy of a system, and the decision to characterise an entity that way is made by those responsible for the system's security. A threat is a motivated, capable adversary: an adversary that is not motivated is not a threat, and neither is one that is motivated but not capable. An attack is an action that attempts to violate the security policy, and a vulnerability is a flaw or weakness in a system's design, implementation or operation that could be exploited to violate it. A countermeasure is a procedure or technique that thwarts an attack, often specific to one attack or class of attack.

Two routing terms carry weight in the analysis. False route origination occurs when a network operator originates a route for a prefix it does not hold and has not been authorised to originate. A route leak occurs when AS-A advertises to its own neighbours routes it received from AS-B, while AS-A is not regarded as a transit provider for those prefixes.

The rest of the definitions describe the RPKI. A certification authority issues digital certificates and vouches for the binding between the data items in a certificate. The RPKI is a public key infrastructure operated by the entities that manage internet number resources, issuing certificates that attest to those holdings. A relying party makes use of signed products from such an infrastructure, verifying them with certificates and certificate revocation lists. The RPKI repository system is a distributed set of loosely synchronised databases, and an RPKI signed object is a data object wrapped in Cryptographic Message Syntax.
sections.plainLanguage: An adversary is someone who might attack, a threat is someone who both might and can, and a vulnerability is a weakness worth exploiting. Route leaks and false origination are the two specific BGP faults the document keeps coming back to.

sections.title: The Adversaries
sections.content:
The RFC names five classes of adversary and is explicit about what each can reach.

Network operators. An operator may be motivated to make its routers emit inaccurate routing information, for example so that traffic flows over paths that are economically better for it. Because the operator controls the routers in its network, it can modify their operation in arbitrary ways, and those routers are vehicles for mounting man-in-the-middle attacks on both control and data plane traffic. If the operator takes part in the RPKI it holds at least one certification authority certificate and may generate subordinate certificates and authorisations of its own, and if it implements path security it will be able to sign updates in a way that its path-security-enabled neighbours accept.

Hackers. A hacker might take control of the management computers and routers of operators, including operators that implement path security, and act as a rogue operator. The RFC assumes hackers generally cannot mount man-in-the-middle attacks on most of the links between networks. They may be motivated by bragging rights, profit or a cause, and are presumed to work remotely rather than from a physical presence at the target.

Criminals. Criminals might persuade an operator, by threat or extortion, to act as a rogue operator, and might persuade the staff of a telecom provider to enable man-in-the-middle attacks on links between routers. Their motives include extorting operators or their clients and manipulating routing to conceal the source of spam or denial-of-service attacks.

Registries. Any registry in the RPKI could be a threat. Registry staff could manipulate repository content or mismanage the certificates they issue, harming an operator or its clients, whether from political pressure in their country or under criminal influence.

Nations. A nation may control network operators in its territory and make them act as rogue operators, may have the technical capability for active wiretapping within its territory, may be able to attack routers or management computers in other countries, and may control a registry such as a regional registry and force it to act in a rogue capacity. The stated motivations are controlling traffic to and from the country and diverting traffic destined for other countries, for passive or active wiretapping including denial of service.
sections.plainLanguage: The adversaries are other operators, hackers, criminals, registry staff and governments. An operator is the hardest case, because it controls its own routers and can sign updates that its neighbours will believe.

sections.title: What the Attacks Look Like
sections.content:
Attacks are grouped by their target. The RFC notes at the outset that attacks of interest try to break the integrity or authenticity of BGP traffic, or the authorisations of the entities in the RPKI; attacks that only break the implied confidentiality of routing traffic are not a requirement for BGP security.

Against the sessions between routers, an active attack can be launched from a remote point or from a position on the link as a man in the middle. The remote form is available to any adversary, while the man-in-the-middle form needs access to the link, and modern transport networks present a large attack surface. Such attacks include replaying selected BGP messages, selectively modifying messages, and denial-of-service attacks against routers.

Against a BGP router, the attacks amount to forging, tampering with or suppressing data inside updates. One important limit is stated up front: behaviour that can be ascribed to a local routing policy decision is not an attack, because it could be explained as a policy choice and is beyond what path security can detect. So a router may fail to propagate some or all withdrawals, or leak routes, and that is not counted here. Within that limit the RFC lists several attacks. A router may insert AS numbers other than its own into an update, which violates BGP and is an attack. It may originate a route for a prefix its AS is not authorised to originate, which is an attack but one the RPKI already addresses. It may remove path data from a protected update before forwarding it to a protected neighbour, which violates the path security goals. It may emit protected data that other routers cannot validate. It may propagate an announcement whose protected data has expired, which is a replay. It may set an expiry time so short that the announcement dies early, which counts as an attack only if the protocol mandates a minimum. And if a private key associated with a router or an AS is compromised, the adversary can generate updates that appear to have passed through that AS.

Against the operator's management computers, compromising a network operations centre computer lets the adversary run any management function the staff could, which changes local routing policy, blackholes routes and more. This behaviour cannot be detected externally as an attack; it just looks like rogue operator behaviour. The same access lets an adversary corrupt the tools that pull data from the RPKI, delete objects from the operator's repository publication point, request revocation of certificates or route origin authorisations, or request router certificates that neighbours will reject.

Against a repository publication point, the RFC considers only attacks by someone who controls a machine hosting publication points but lacks the keys needed to produce valid signed products. Because everything in a repository is signed, such attacks turn into denial-of-service attacks. Relying parties cache what they fetch, so they can detect deleted products, products with bad signatures, tampered signatures and replacements of newer objects with older valid ones, and they can fall back on their cache. Deleting a manifest is detectable, and the relying party can keep using the last valid copy. Deleting newly added certificates and replacing the manifest with the previous one leaves the manifest and its certificate revocation list stale, which alerts the relying party, which is expected to use a Ghostbusters Record to contact the publication point maintainer and ask for a remedy. The RFC notes that staleness is only detected once the next issue date passes, which is why certificate revocation list and manifest lifetimes have to balance risk against operational burden.

Against an RPKI certification authority, the attack surface is different: the private key need not be disclosed at all. If the adversary controls the machine that issues certificates, it can revoke or replace any certificate the authority has issued, which makes the routes that depend on them less preferred without being detectable by most relying parties. The RFC notes that most of these attacks are easier to recover from when the authority is a victim rather than the adversary, which motivates hardware security modules for the keys of the higher tiers. A controlling adversary can also create subordinate certificates that send relying parties on a wild goose chase, publish certificates with very brief validity, create very large numbers of authorisations, or issue certificates with overlapping allocations to different entities. One limit does apply: the extensions in RFC 3779 prevent a compromised authority from issuing valid certificates for resources outside its own scope.
sections.plainLanguage: The attacks fall into four groups: breaking the link between routers, tampering with a router, tampering with the operator's own management machines, and tampering with the repository and the authority that fills it. Signing makes most repository attacks obvious, but obvious does not mean harmless.

sections.title: Residual Vulnerabilities
sections.content:
Some weaknesses survive even with path security and the RPKI, and the RFC lists them.

The first is that the repository system may be attacked in ways that make its contents unavailable, out of date or inconsistent. The main defence is the local cache each relying party keeps, which preserves previously acquired data when a repository is unreachable or its contents are deleted. The system still cannot guarantee that every relying party has access to up-to-date data, and when one detects a problem it has two choices. It can keep using its cache, tolerating expired or stale objects, which exposes it to attacks that rely on its ignorance of changes. Or it can purge the expired objects, which removes the security information attached to the real-world resources concerned. That is the same as those resources never having been protected, and because use of the RPKI and path security is voluntary, purging effectively moves them into the set of unprotected resources. This lets an attacker move resources from the protected set to the unprotected set.

The second is that any authority in the RPKI may misbehave within the bounds of the resources allocated to it, for example by issuing certificates with duplicate resource allocations or revoking certificates inappropriately. The RFC calls this intrinsic to any public key infrastructure, and notes that its impact is limited in the RPKI by the extensions in RFC 3779, with administrative action expected to handle it once detected.

Path security has its own residual weaknesses. Route leaks are a routing security problem for many operators, but BGP itself has no semantics that preclude them and no RFC defines the term, so the RFC does not address them and notes the document should be revised if the security context is later revised to include them. Path security is not required to protect every attribute associated with an AS path, even though some are used as routing inputs, so attacks that modify or strip those other attributes are not prevented or detected. Confederation members that are not represented in the path are not a concern, because they are not externally visible and so do not influence route selection. Finally, path security cannot ensure that an AS withdraws a route when it no longer has one; it may bound the lifetime of an advertisement, which caps how long such a failure remains effective.
sections.plainLanguage: Some problems stay. If the repository goes stale, a router either trusts old data or drops the protection entirely. Route leaks and the other attributes of a path are outside what this design covers.

sections.title: What a Threat Model Is For
sections.content: The RFC closes with a statement of what its own kind of document is. A threat model is, by definition, a security-centric document. Unlike a protocol description it does not create security problems, nor does it claim to address them. It postulates a set of threats, that is motivated and capable adversaries, examines the classes of attack those threats can mount based on their motivations, describes the impact on path security and on the RPKI that path security relies on, notes where the design of the RPKI and the goals of path security already address classes of attack, and records the residual vulnerabilities.
sections.plainLanguage: A threat model is not a protocol and does not fix anything. It sets out who might attack, what they would try, and what the design already handles, so that the people writing the protocol know where the edges are.

items.title: Network operators
items.text: They control their own routers, can send inaccurate updates, and can sign updates that protected neighbours accept.

items.title: Hackers
items.text: They may take over management computers and routers and act as rogue operators, but cannot usually tap links directly.

items.title: Criminals
items.text: They may coerce operators or telecom staff, and may manipulate routing to hide spam and denial-of-service attacks.

items.title: Registries
items.text: Staff can manipulate repository content or mismanage the certificates they issue, for political or criminal reasons.

items.title: Nations
items.text: They may control operators and registries in their territory, tap traffic inside it, and attack routers elsewhere.

items.label: AS Insertion
items.desc: A router puts AS numbers other than its own into an update, which violates BGP.

items.label: False Route Origination
items.desc: A router originates a route for a prefix its AS is not authorised to originate. The RPKI addresses this.

items.label: Secure Path Downgrade
items.desc: A router strips path data from a protected update before passing it to a protected neighbour.

items.label: Invalid Path Data Insertion
items.desc: A router emits protected data that other routers cannot validate.

items.label: Stale Path Announcement
items.desc: An expired protected announcement is passed on, which is a replay.

items.label: Premature Expiration
items.desc: A router sets an expiry time so short that the announcement dies early.

items.label: MITM Attack
items.desc: A link-protection key is compromised, letting the attacker sit in the middle of the link.

items.label: Compromised Private Key
items.desc: A router or AS key is stolen, letting the adversary forge updates that look genuine.
